sections.title: How Switches Work + VLANs
sections.content:
A switch learns which MAC address lives on which port (building a MAC address table) and forwards frames only out the correct port. Unknown-destination and broadcast frames are flooded to all ports in the VLAN.
VLAN (Virtual LAN) — logically segments one physical switch into separate broadcast domains. Hosts in different VLANs can't talk without a router/Layer-3 switch (inter-VLAN routing). Benefits: segmentation, security, less broadcast traffic.
Access port — carries one VLAN, connects to an end device.
Trunk port — carries many VLANs between switches, tagging frames with 802.1Q. The native VLAN on a trunk is sent untagged.
Voice VLAN — a separate VLAN for IP phones on the same port as a PC.
exam_tips: VLANs separate broadcast domains; you need a router or Layer-3 switch to route between them.
802.1Q is the trunking/VLAN-tagging standard. The native VLAN is untagged.
Access port = one VLAN to a device; trunk port = many VLANs between switches.

sections.title: Spanning Tree & Redundancy
sections.content:
Redundant switch links create loops, and loops cause broadcast storms. STP (Spanning Tree Protocol, 802.1D) prevents them by blocking redundant paths, leaving one active path; if the active link fails, a blocked one activates.
Key terms: the root bridge is elected (lowest bridge ID); ports become root/designated (forwarding) or blocking. RSTP (802.1w) converges faster.
Port roles/features: PortFast moves access ports straight to forwarding; BPDU Guard disables a port that unexpectedly receives STP BPDUs (protects against rogue switches).
Link aggregation (LACP / 802.3ad) bundles multiple physical links into one logical link for more bandwidth and redundancy.
exam_tips: STP prevents switching loops/broadcast storms by blocking redundant links.
Link aggregation (LACP/802.3ad) combines ports for bandwidth + redundancy.
BPDU Guard protects access ports from rogue switches sending BPDUs.

sections.title: PoE, Port Security & Switch Features
sections.content:
PoE (Power over Ethernet) delivers power + data over one cable to APs, phones, cameras.
802.3af (PoE) ~15.4W · 802.3at (PoE+) ~30W · 802.3bt (PoE++) up to ~60–100W. Budget the switch's total PoE wattage across ports.
Port security — limits which/how many MAC addresses a port accepts; can shut down on violation (stops MAC flooding and rogue devices).
MAC filtering, DHCP snooping (blocks rogue DHCP servers), and dynamic ARP inspection harden the access layer.
Jumbo frames (MTU ~9000) boost throughput for storage/data-center links.
MDIX/Auto-MDIX auto-detects straight-through vs crossover.
exam_tips: Port security limits MACs per port and can disable the port on violation.
DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP servers; dynamic ARP inspection stops ARP spoofing.

concept_cards.hook: A Virtual LAN that logically splits a switch into separate broadcast domains; inter-VLAN traffic needs a router or Layer-3 switch.
A switch link that carries multiple VLANs by tagging frames with a VLAN ID; the native VLAN is sent untagged.
Prevents switching loops by blocking redundant links, keeping one active path and failing over if it breaks.
Bundling several physical links (802.3ad) into one logical connection for added bandwidth and redundancy.
A switch feature limiting which or how many MAC addresses a port accepts, able to disable the port on a violation.
Power over Ethernet standards delivering power with data: 802.3af ~15W, 802.3at ~30W, 802.3bt up to ~100W.
A switch security feature that trusts DHCP replies only from approved ports, blocking rogue DHCP servers.
A flood of broadcast/looped frames that saturates a switched network; prevented by Spanning Tree Protocol.

practice_questions.q: Which protocol tags frames to carry multiple VLANs over one trunk link?
practice_questions.explanation: 802.1Q inserts a VLAN tag into Ethernet frames on trunk links.

practice_questions.q: What must be configured to allow devices in different VLANs to communicate?
practice_questions.explanation: VLANs are separate broadcast domains; routing between them requires a router or Layer 3 switch.

practice_questions.q: Which feature protects an access port by disabling it if it receives STP BPDUs?
practice_questions.explanation: BPDU Guard shuts a port that unexpectedly receives BPDUs, blocking rogue switches.

practice_questions.q: Which switch feature moves an access port directly to forwarding, skipping STP listening/learning?
practice_questions.explanation: PortFast speeds up end-device ports by bypassing the STP transitional states.

practice_questions.q: What is the main purpose of Spanning Tree Protocol?
options: Prevent switching loops on redundant links
practice_questions.explanation: STP blocks redundant paths to avoid loops and broadcast storms.

practice_questions.q: A switch receives a frame for an unknown destination MAC. What does it do?
options: Floods it out all ports in the VLAN except the source
Sends it only to the default gateway
practice_questions.explanation: Unknown-unicast frames are flooded within the VLAN until the switch learns the MAC.

practice_questions.q: Which standard delivers up to ~100W over Ethernet?
practice_questions.explanation: 802.3bt (PoE++) supplies up to ~60–100W; af is ~15W and at is ~30W.

practice_questions.q: An MTU of ~9000 bytes used to boost throughput on storage links describes:
practice_questions.explanation: Jumbo frames carry ~9000-byte payloads to reduce overhead on high-throughput links.

practice_questions.q: Which feature validates that DHCP replies come only from trusted ports?
practice_questions.explanation: DHCP snooping permits DHCP server replies only on configured trusted ports, blocking rogue servers.

practice_questions.q: Two switches must carry multiple VLANs over a single link. What should the link be configured as?
practice_questions.explanation: Trunk ports carry multiple VLANs between switches by tagging frames with 802.1Q.
